title: WHEN BUILDINGS DON'T WORK: THE ROLE OF ARCHITECTURE IN HUMAN HEALTH
authors: Gary W. Evans and Janetta Mitchell McCoy, 1998
central_proposition: Building design has the potential to cause psychological stress, which can eventually affect human health, and this paper proposes a taxonomy of architectural dimensions that contribute to this stress.

concept_definitions.name: Stress
concept_definitions.definition: An imbalance of environmental demands and human resources.

concept_definitions.name: Stimulation
concept_definitions.definition: The amount of information in a setting or object that impinges upon the human user, characterized by intensity, variety, complexity, mystery, and novelty.

concept_definitions.name: Coherence
concept_definitions.definition: The clarity or comprehensibility of building elements and form, impeded by ambiguity, disorganization, and disorientation.

concept_definitions.name: Affordances
concept_definitions.definition: The functional properties a space provides, and the information systems that provide feedback about building or equipment performance; misaffordances occur when these are not readily discernible or are incorrectly gauged.

concept_definitions.name: Control
concept_definitions.definition: Mastery or the ability to either alter the physical environment or regulate exposure to one's surroundings, influenced by physical constraints, flexibility, responsiveness, privacy, spatial syntax, defensible space, and symbolic elements.

concept_definitions.name: Restorative Qualities
concept_definitions.definition: The potential of design elements to function therapeutically, reducing cognitive fatigue and other sources of stress by providing resources that attenuate stress.

concept_definitions.name: Legibility
concept_definitions.definition: The ease with which one can comprehend the spatial configuration of an interior space.

concept_definitions.name: Responsiveness
concept_definitions.definition: The clarity and speed of feedback one receives when acting upon a setting or object.

concept_definitions.name: Privacy
concept_definitions.definition: The ability to regulate social interaction.

concept_definitions.name: Territoriality
concept_definitions.definition: Jurisdiction over space, enhanced by surveillance opportunities, delineated boundaries, semi-public spaces, and smaller subunits.

argument_structure: The paper introduces the concept of psychological stress as a heuristic to understand how the built environment affects human health. It then defines five architectural dimensions (Stimulation, Coherence, Affordances, Control, and Restorative qualities), elaborating on specific interior design elements within each dimension and linking them to stress-related outcomes. The argument is built by defining each dimension, explaining its mechanism for influencing stress, and providing illustrative design examples.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The overarching causal logic is that certain architectural dimensions and their constituent design elements can either increase environmental demands or deplete human coping resources, leading to an imbalance that manifests as psychological stress. Chronic or acute stress, in turn, is proposed to negatively impact human physical and psychological health. Restorative elements are proposed to function as coping resources, attenuating stress.

findings.antecedent: Extremes of stimulus intensity, very complex, or incoherent patterns of stimulation (e.g., loud noise, bright light, strong smells, bright colors, crowding, close interpersonal distances)
findings.mechanism: Causes distraction and overload, interfering with cognitive processes that demand effort or concentration, or leads to boredom/sensory deprivation by depriving the organism of practice in accommodating environmental challenges.
findings.source: Linking Architectural Dimensions to Stress - Stimulation
findings.quote: Extremes of stimulus intensity and very complex or incoherent patterns of stimulation are potentially stress-inducing.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Wohlwill (1974), Berlyne (1971), Mehrabian & Russell (1974), Aiello (1987), Baum & Paulus (1987)

findings.antecedent: Too much complexity or mystery in interiors
findings.mechanism: Makes prediction trivial or difficult, challenging human cognitive capacities to make sense of the environment.
findings.source: Linking Architectural Dimensions to Stress - Stimulation
findings.quote: Too much complexity or mystery makes interiors confusing and unanalyzable; too little renders prediction trivial

findings.antecedent: Incoherence (ambiguity, disorganization, disorientation, mixed/ambiguous cues, conflicting information, abrupt shifts in design elements)
findings.mechanism: Makes prediction difficult, hinders discernment of underlying form/pattern, prevents people from making sense of their environment (meaning, function, basic form).
findings.source: Linking Architectural Dimensions to Stress - Coherence
findings.quote: Stress can occur when changes or disruptions in physical surroundings make prediction difficult. Incoherence can also arise from disorganization

findings.antecedent: Legibility (regular geometric building shapes, distinctive interior markings, views of external environment, good signage, landmarks at decision nodes/path termini, circulation patterns aligned with facades/right angles, visual cues toward goal points)
findings.mechanism: Increases the ease with which one can comprehend the spatial configuration of an interior space, allowing users to make reasonable deductions about identity, meaning, and location.
findings.source: Linking Architectural Dimensions to Stress - Coherence
findings.quote: Legibility, the ease with which one can comprehend the spatial configuration of an interior space, is a critical component of building coherence.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Weisman (1982), Evans (1980), Garling et al. (1986), Passini (1984), Zimring & Gross (1991), Appleyard (1976), Carpman et al. (1986)

findings.antecedent: Misaffordances (ambiguous/conflicting information about functional meaning, rapid changes in visual access, vague/missing/competing cues for use, lack of feedback, user-designer mental model gap)
findings.mechanism: Inability to readily discern the functional properties of a space or incorrectly gauge building/technological function, leading to negative emotional and behavioral responses.
findings.source: Linking Architectural Dimensions to Stress - Affordances
findings.quote: When we are unable to readily discern the func-tional properties of a space or incorrectly gauge building or technological function, misaffordances occur

findings.antecedent: Reduced control (physical constraints, insufficient spatial resources, inflexible spatial arrangements, lack of climatic/lighting controls, unresponsive environments, lack of privacy, institutional quality, lack of territoriality)
findings.consequent: Psychological stress, learned helplessness, psychological distress, physical disease, powerlessness
findings.mechanism: Reduces choice or behavioral options, leading to prolonged experiences with uncontrollable environmental conditions, which are linked to learned helplessness and its associated negative health outcomes.
findings.source: Linking Architectural Dimensions to Stress - Control
findings.quote: Physical constraints that reduce choice or behavioral options can produce or exacerbate stress
findings.empirical_support_cited: Glass & Singer (1972), Evans & Cohen (1987), Cohen et al. (1986), Peterson et al. (1993), Hedge (1991), Sherrod & Cohen (1979), Rivlin & Wolfe (1985)

findings.antecedent: Responsiveness (clarity and speed of feedback, differential feedback, short latency between actions and feedback)
findings.mechanism: Provides clear and timely information about the consequences of one's actions on a setting or object, preventing feelings of helplessness.
findings.source: Linking Architectural Dimensions to Stress - Control
findings.quote: Responsiveness refers to the clarity and speed of feedback one receives when act-ing upon a setting or object
findings.empirical_support_cited: Wachs (1989), Wohlwill & Heft (1987), Cohen et al. (1986)

findings.antecedent: Privacy (spatial hierarchy, size, location, stimulus isolation, depth of spaces, functional distance, well-designed focal points, sociopetal furniture arrangements)
findings.consequent: Sense of control, ability to regulate social interaction
findings.mechanism: Allows individuals to manage their social interactions and exposure to others, which is a major contributor to a sense of control.
findings.source: Linking Architectural Dimensions to Stress - Control
findings.quote: Privacy, or the ability to regulate social inter-action, is a major contributor to a sense of control in interior settings
findings.empirical_support_cited: Altman (1975), Alexander (1972), Greenbie (1981), Zimring (1982), Hillier & Hanson (1984), Archea (1977), Festinger et al. (1950), Sommer (1969), Bechtel (1976), Becker (1990)

findings.antecedent: Territoriality (jurisdiction over space, good surveillance opportunities, clearly delineated and visibly marked boundaries, semi-public spaces, smaller subunits of large living complexes)
findings.consequent: Feelings of territoriality, regulated use/occupancy of space, expression of personal/group identity
findings.mechanism: Enables regulated use and occupancy of space and allows for the expression of personal or group identity, contributing to a sense of control.
findings.source: Linking Architectural Dimensions to Stress - Control
findings.quote: Territoriality enables regulated use and occupancy of space. It also enhances the expression of personal or group identity

findings.antecedent: Restorative design elements (privacy nooks, stimulus shelters, window views, burning fireplaces, various displays, direct contact with natural elements, views of nature)
findings.mechanism: Provide resources that attenuate stress, replenish cognitive capacity, and foster involuntary attention or fascination, allowing for mental rest, recovery, or contemplation.
findings.source: Linking Architectural Dimensions to Stress - Restorative
findings.quote: Restorative elements provide resources that can attenuate stress. Thus design can function as a coping resource that can help building occu-pants alter the balance between environmental demands and personal resources.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Wachs & Gruen (1982), Kaplan & Kaplan (1989), Coss (1973), Hartig & Evans (1993), Ulrich (1993)

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Environments with extreme levels of stimulation (too high or too low) will lead to increased physiological stress markers (e.g., cortisol, heart rate variability) and decreased cognitive performance (e.g., attention, concentration) compared to environments with moderate stimulation.

Incoherent interior spaces, characterized by ambiguity, disorganization, or disorientation, will result in higher self-reported stress and frustration, and slower wayfinding times, than legible and coherent spaces.
The presence of misaffordances in a built environment will lead to increased self-reported frustration, annoyance, and feelings of helplessness among users.

Environments designed with low perceived control (e.g., inflexible layouts, lack of personalizable elements, poor privacy) will correlate with higher levels of psychological distress and self-reported powerlessness among occupants.

Exposure to restorative design elements (e.g., views of nature, designated retreat spaces) will facilitate faster recovery from directed attention fatigue and reduce physiological stress responses following a demanding cognitive task.
bridge_warrants: The paper explicitly links its framework to established theories of psychological stress (Cohen et al., 1995; Evans & Cohen, 1987) as the primary mechanism for health impacts.
The concept of learned helplessness (Cohen et al., 1986; Peterson et al., 1993) is directly integrated to explain the consequences of reduced environmental control.

The discussion of stimulation, complexity, and mystery draws upon work by Kaplan & Kaplan (1982, 1989), implicitly connecting to Attention Restoration Theory (ART) and theories of environmental preference.

The restorative dimension directly references Stress Recovery Theory (Ulrich, 1993) and Attention Restoration Theory (Kaplan & Kaplan, 1989) as mechanisms for stress attenuation and cognitive replenishment.
The concept of affordances is rooted in ecological psychology (Heft, 1997) and human-computer interaction (Norman, 1989), providing a link to embodied cognition and user experience.
The discussion of privacy and territoriality connects to Altman's (1975) privacy regulation theory and related work on social interaction and personal space.
methodological_critiques: A major weakness of our taxonomy is the lack of empirical evidence linking the design elements we have identified to human health. At present the knowledge base is simply not there.

Most existing research on stress and ill health has focused on personal variables (e.g., Type A behavior) or social conditions (e.g., social support), with little attention paid to the built environment's role.
model_structure: The paper proposes a preliminary taxonomy of five architectural dimensions (Stimulation, Coherence, Affordances, Control, Restorative) that are hypothesized to influence human health by altering psychological stress levels. Each dimension is further broken down into specific interior design elements. The model suggests a causal pathway from specific design features to stress, and then from stress to human health outcomes.
limitations: The taxonomy is derived primarily from the heuristic of psychological stress, which is only one of several underlying processes that could explain how the built environment affects human health (e.g., negative emotions like anxiety/depression, health promotion activities like safety compliance or lifestyle alterations).
There is a significant lack of existing empirical evidence directly linking the specific design elements identified in this taxonomy to human health outcomes.
